extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, and graduate students in mass communication
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and theoretical criteria for what makes events and actors become news and how structural, organizational, and ideological forces shape news content; guidance for designing media-content research across multiple levels of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market size affects coverage of spontaneous and local events
rubrics_metrics.description: The larger the market, the more the media will cover spontaneous news events and local news. The presence of a competing newspaper, however, apparently does not increase diversity in newspaper content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger audience markets stimulate more immediate/local coverage; competition (a competing newspaper) may not by itself diversify content. Use market-size as a predictor of emphasis on spontaneous/local items when analyzing news output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic coverage breadth increases content standardization
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider the geographic area a medium covers, the more standardized its content will be. Messages must be broadened to appeal to people with varying interests and tastes. Such content will take few chances and make few innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a medium targets a broad or geographically dispersed audience, expect conservative, risk-averse, non-innovative reporting designed to appeal to many; consider geographic scope when assessing originality or variation in content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviance increases likelihood of inclusion and stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: The more deviant people or events are, the more likely they are to be included in media content and the more likely they are to be stereotyped. The media help maintain the boundaries of social order by showing what is approved and not approved. Deviant people and events may be trivialized or shown as dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measures of perceived deviance to predict both inclusion and patterning (e.g., stereotyping, trivialization, threat framing) in coverage; applies cross-nationally in U.S. media analyses. Examine both selection and representational framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nation-to-nation significance determines foreign-coverage priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The more political, economic, or cultural significance one country has for another, the more the former will appear in the latter's mass media. Such social system-level attachments between countries affect priorities in media coverage. Although the same news values may apply for domestic and foreign news coverage, measures of political, economic, and cultural significance affect what is considered important, one of the main criteria for establishing newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating foreign news presence, incorporate measures of bilateral political/economic/cultural ties as predictors of coverage volume and prominence; newsworthiness is shaped by these system-level attachments in addition to standard news values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective routines (e.g., balance) are situationally applied
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists will not use objective routines, such as balance, when subjects are outside the area of legitimate controversy and in the areas of consensus or deviance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume journalistic routines like 'balance' are universally applied; examine whether an issue falls inside legitimate controversy. In areas of consensus or clear deviance, expect different uses (or abandonment) of formal objectivity routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite collective response when core ideological principles are threatened
rubrics_metrics.description: Elites will respond to media as a class when core ideological principles are threatened. Actions of business, for example, will be more unified and coordinated, transcending the actions of any given company or industry, as more capitalist values come under attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze elite behavior at a class level (not only individual firms) when media coverage implicates foundational ideological commitments; expect coordinated strategies and unified messaging in defense of core values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite institutional connections shape media ideological consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The more closely media are connected to other elites, the more media content will be consistent with those elite ideological view-points. Examples of elite connections include board interlocks and club memberships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure formal and informal ties between media organizations and elite institutions (board membership, clubs, business ties) to predict ideological alignment in coverage; such ties increase content consonance with elite viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational paradigm violations are repaired to preserve the paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of occupational paradigms—anomalies—must be repaired in order to preserve the paradigm. This repair is most evident when the violation crosses important ideological boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect corrective processes (reframing, marginalization, disciplinary actions) when journalistic norms are breached, especially if the breach challenges dominant ideological boundaries; include mechanisms of repair in analyses of newsroom response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television coverage tends to be more ideologically charged than print
rubrics_metrics.description: On a given issue, television coverage will be more ideologically charged than the print media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing media platforms, anticipate greater ideological intensity on television; account for medium-specific tendencies in cross-platform content comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multi-level (hierarchy of influences) analysis; avoid single-level overgeneralization
rubrics_metrics.description: By approaching media studies from several levels, we can better appreciate the different perspectives that are possible. Any single perspective does not present a complete picture, and any given study cannot address all these levels at once. But an awareness of these multiple perspectives helps keep our thinking open. Many studies make observations at one level of analysis and interpret those findings at a higher level. For example, many scholars have examined individual journalists and then drawn conclusions about media organizations as a whole. Individual bias, however, does not translate automatically into media bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design research to recognize levels (individual, routine, organizational, extra-media, ideological/system) and be cautious about extrapolating from one level to another; explicitly state level of inference and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and test interlevel links (connect micro and macro influences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining these multiple levels of analysis draws our attention to the connections between them. Occupational routines are related to larger ideological requirements. Personal values of journalists cannot be separated from their routines. Organizational structure is related to media routines, and so on. Ideological forces must work through people and practices, and finding out how that happens is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize empirical work that maps how higher-level forces (ideology, organizational structure) operate through meso- and micro-level mechanisms (routines, individual values); build hypotheses and measures that trace causal or correlational chains across levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek theoretical and methodological precision for media-content research
rubrics_metrics.description: Until recently, in mainstream U.S. media research, the greatest theoretical and methodological precision has been found in the studies of mass communication processes and effects. We hope that the same kind of precision and systematic study can be directed at media content and the influences on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the rigorous theoretical framing and methodological standards used in process/effect research when studying content — e.g., clear operationalization, careful sampling, and precise measurement — to advance cumulative knowledge about news content influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition ideological-level studies on empirical knowledge of individuals and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: We hope that even studies at the lower levels of analysis will be informed by the theories of power and society developed at the higher levels, and that ideological-level studies will be conditioned by an understanding of individuals and their practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal conditioning: let macro theories inform micro studies and let micro empirical findings temper macro/ideological claims. Explicitly integrate individual/practice-level data when making ideological-level assertions.
